title: Neuhaus Metalworks Solstice Hardtail Review: Nothing More, Nothing Less – John Watson & Kyle Klain
content:
Ever since his 2023 Shop Visit, in which he first laid eyes on the Neuhaus Solstice prototype, John has wanted to get his grubby mitts on one to ride. Once the production run of frames landed from Taiwan, the team at Neuhaus Metalworks sent a Solstice frame, fork, and brakes out for him to build up. He took this opportunity to build the ideal metal hardtail; nothing more, nothing less…

Looking back to over three years ago, I had just wrapped up a ride in China Camp with Nick Neuhaus aboard a size XL Hummingbird hardtail. We’d done one of Nick’s favorite loops and were resting by a picturesque tree, surrounded by California poppies, talking shop. Nick’s partner with Neuhaus, Daniel Yang, was just getting over a cold, so he couldn’t ride with us, but he met up after the ride, and with him, he brought his Solstice prototype hardtail.

At the time, all Neuhaus frames were made in California, but since that 2023 Shop Visit, Neuhaus has moved to manufacturing its “Core” line in Taiwan. This includes a Core Hummingbird and Core Solstice. Nick still builds custom bikes out of his Novato-based shop.

The XC-oriented Hummingbird, left, and the more trail-ready Solstice, right…

While the 120 mm travel Hummingbird was arguably a little too undergunned for my riding style and preference, the Solstice looked very appetizing. Little did I know that I wouldn’t get to ride one for three years. Earlier this year, that day finally came in the shape of a Neuhaus frame box with a Fox 36 SL Performance Grip fork and TRP brakes.

Hailey wrote a phenomenal review of the Hummingbird; I recommend you read it if a 120 mm travel bike is more your style…

Solstice Review Build Logic

When you run a cycling website, you accumulate parts from previous review bikes and purchases over time. That’s definitely the case for me. I move through bikes at a steady cadence, but this year, I reeled back the number of review bikes I took on, hoping to spend more quality time with a few models, rather than run through bikes at my normal frequency.

The Solstice was a bike that demanded some attention with its build kit. I wanted to build a hardtail that embodies my view of a bomber, all-metal build kit.

Nothing More, Nothing Less

Looking at my parts bin, mostly leftover from the Sour Cowboy Cookie, a bike I still dream about, I took the wide and strong Astral Serpentine wheels, wrapped in Schwalbe’s award-winning Radial tires, along with the Ratio Mech, titanium Lucky Riser Doom bars, a 22.2 Paul Boxcar stem, and those killer Cyber Cycles steel cranks. The 220 mm travel dropper post just made the bike look all the more capable. When I sent Daniel Yang an initial build photo, he replied with “Nice! Slick build, massive dropper!”

Long-leggedness aside, I’d quite liked all of the gear leftover from the Sour build and felt like sticking with a mostly familiar build kit could help me isolate what exactly that slender steel frame would be doing under my legs as I lightfootedly pedaled it all over the Santa Fe National Forest.

While this is by no means close to how Neuhaus would spec one of its complete frame offerings, for me, it balances capable but steezy parts that are as good-looking as they are reliable. And increases the shreddy nature of a 130-travel hardtail frame.

Before we get into that, let’s break it down.

Neuhaus Solstice Quick Hits

  • $1,299 frame
  • $1,899 frame and Fox 36 SL Performance Grip fork (discounted price; recommended)
  • Made in Taiwan
  • S-XL (XL reviewed here)
  • XL frame weight: 6.7 lbs with the cable clips, seatpost clamp, and rear axle
  • 32 lbs complete as shown for size XL with an all-metal build including steel cranks
  • 65° HTA
  • 130 mm travel
  • 29″ wheels with 2.6″ clearance
  • Quad-butted, heat-treated 4130 Steel

Daniel Yang and Nick Neuhaus collaborated on the Neuhaus Metalworks line, and the Solstice, to me, embodies what I would call the perfect hardtail platform. It’s designed for 130 mm of travel with a geometry that is neither too progressive nor too XC. Neuhaus recommends you build it with big brakes, burly tires, and a stout fork. When combined together, its pleasantly compliant steel chassis creates one of the best riding experiences I’ve had from a Taiwan-made frame.

Rider Profile

I’m a big dude at 6’2″, 210 lbs, with long legs and long arms. In these photos, my saddle height is 83 cm. My riding is exclusive to primitive and technical singletrack. Steep up, steep down, loose, chunky, with a few moments of respite found in some “flowy” sections. In terms of riding style, I like to actively use the trail, hitting different lines each ride and jibbing all the way down. I prefer frames with some flex and usually avoid overly stiff bikes. I live in Santa Fe, New Mexico, at 7200′ in the Rocky Mountains. Most of my riding these days is in the Santa Fe National Forest.

Solstice Geometry

Hell fuckin’ yes, praise to the Necronomicog, someone made a proper ETT for a size XL. Knowing exactly how I like my bikes to fit and sizing them off ETT – sorry, Travis – I was elated to see the Solstice’s size XL come with a whopping 674 mm ETT. Other notes that caused pause were the 65º head angle, another metric perfect for this class of MTB, and a 74.5º seat tube angle, which, for the sake of the Solstice’s designed terrain – the Bay Area – felt modest, without being too progressive. More on that later.

The Doom Lucky Riser bars and a modest 2 cm of spacers under the stem brought the bars close to being level with my saddle, a metric that helps with understanding stack height’s relationship to its rider. I’m still waiting on Spencer’s Dust-Up on that topic! The Solstice has a 150 mm head tube, which is a welcome change from previous size XL bikes I’d ridden with 130 mm head tubes. The top headset cup is external, with the lower headset bearing internal. As a long-legged fella with an 83 cm saddle height and 175 mm cranks, the bike has a certain steeze that is undeniable for a seemingly conservative hardtail package.

Solstice Frame Details

Neuhaus frames lack ostentation. There aren’t details that stand out from the sea of steel hardtails, save for two areas: the chainstay yoke and stand-off seat tube bottle bosses. I’ve long lauded the brand’s eye for proportions. The tubing diameters look neither too slender nor too beefy. The bike can fit two bottles in all sizes, with the larger sizes eking out two large bottles. Thanks to the seat tube bottle mount, you don’t have to worry about your dropper post hitting bottle bosses either.

Chainstay yokes maintain enough clearance for 2.6″ tires and 38-tooth chainrings. The frame is 1x compatible only, as most modern hardtails are; it’s optimized for 1x drivetrains, and the Solstice uses a UDH dropout design. The yoke also provides a nice “sand shelf” to display your recent soil accumulations. Loam, dust, or sand. Your pick!

A beautiful, Tapered IS42/52 head tube omits external cups in favor of hidden bearings, IS brake mounts allow for big rotors with the use of an adapter, and a 73 mm BSA bottom bracket shell keeps it simple. The cable management is nice and tidy with M5 bolt-on cable cradling on the underside of the top and down tube.

It’s an incredibly well-thought-out frame, considering hardtails are one of the simplest off-road phenotypes. In fact, my only request for the Solstice V2 is more seat stay bridge clearance, as with my 2.6″ measured tires, the occasional rock gets picked up and pings against the bridge.

Cotta Frame Flex

Using our Pasta Cook metric for frame flex, I was pleasantly surprised by the Solstice’s flex. Granted, I’m on the size XL with the 674 mm ETT, so it’s a long bike. Sitting on the saddle and swaying hips side to side delivers a comfortable amount of wiggle, but not so much that the bike gets lost underfoot in steep and rocky terrain. It’s the “right” amount of flex for a bike that has no rack mounts, in my opinion. Neuhaus didn’t design it for bike camping; they designed it for comfortable compliance during everyday rides.

I reached out to Nick Neuhaus and asked him what his intent was with the Solstice frame flex:

“We designed each size to have similar ride feel across the size range. Our goal is for every size rider to have the same experience with their bike. A rider on a medium should get the same feeling from their bike that you get from an XL. ”

At the end of the day, I never felt like I was fighting the frame in the chunk or pressing against a stiff chassis. Nor did I feel any noticeable heft while climbing. And while bike weight isn’t a real concern for me, a rider pushing 210 lbs with all his gear on, I would put this frame in line with US-made hardtails I’ve ridden that were designed specifically for my weight and riding style.

Taiwan-made frames often err on the stouter side because the manufacturer designs them for the masses. Yet the Neuhaus pushes in the opposite direction, designing around frame feel and flex and keeping it lean and mean.

Neuhaus Solstice on Climbing

Now, I do believe that bike weight doesn’t matter in a subjective way, but having a light-feeling frame under you while you tackle a 5,000′ climb is objectively an added bonus. With my full-metal build kit, I opted for the Schwalbe Magic Mary and Albert combination I lauded on my Meriwether. This tire combination allows for endless gecko-like grip when scaling our chunderous climbs in the Southern Rockies. While climbing over springtime post-monsoon wet roots, slick rocks, and damp soil, or the dregs of a dry summer where everything was blown out, the Radial tires found purchase and the Solstice’s geometry felt familiar.

Most modern bikes are hovering around a 77º seat tube angle. On a full-suspension bike, you sag into a rear shock and a front fork, but on a hardtail, a static, non-sagged 74.5º seat angle steepens with front-fork sag. Neuhaus lists its geo unsagged, so when the trail got steep and techy, perched on the nose of the saddle, I could dig in over the bottom bracket more to climb efficiently.

Frame design is a part of the whole equation, and as the seat angle steepened, so did the head angle, which made it easy to flick and maneuver the front end when needed as well. The 56 mm of BB drop kept the 175 mm cranks mostly free of pedal strike as well. Long cranks are left out of the conversation in most bike media, and if you haven’t figured out how to ratchet your pedals through techy sections, it’d be a good thing to learn. Pedal strikes are always avoidable.

I’d hate to have the Solstice’s BB go any higher or lower, for that matter, because this bike is a fucking beast on the descents.

Unhinged, Psychotic Descents

Wide bars, supple fork, grippy tires, compliant wheels, and a thousand-yard stare down the trail, and the Solstice, even only having 130 mm of travel, becomes a veritable plow on the descents. On trails I’d normally want to tap on the brakes on similar-travel spec bikes, for some reason I wanted to push my limits harder on the Solstice. Coming right off the Revel Rascal review period, I was nervous I’d be missing the Rascal’s calm and centered demeanor, but by contrast, the Solstice felt inherently scrappy and would roll up its sleeves every time I pointed it downhill.

There isn’t a world where I’d request even the slightest geo tweak with this bike. It hammers on techy trails, and when there’s a trailside booter, like the ones often featured in my bike reviews that are found on my lunch lap, it enjoys being aloft. I hadn’t ridden a hardtail that liked to get aloft since the Viral Derive. And a lot of that has to do with Nick Neuhaus’ background in BMX and dirt jumpers. He likes a higher BB because it makes the bike more flickable, going against the modern parlance of a “long, slack, low” approach to geometry where a lower bottom bracket puts you more “in” the bike; the Solstice feels like you’re riding atop it like a dirt jumper.

Insert Synonym for Confidence-Inspiring Here

A lot of this camaraderie I felt with the Solstice had to do with the parts spec as delivered from Neuhaus. Yes, I supplied the cockpit and drivetrain, but Nick and Daniel from Neuhaus encourage people to use the TRP brakes and Fox 36 SL Performance Grip fork. Their reasoning follows my own thoughts around riding Mavens on a hardtail: the more raw power, the better.

High-speed descending requires immediate power for when the line choice goes pear-shaped. I definitely pushed myself riding the Solstice and was always thankful for the bite of the TRP calipers, delivered by the slightest pull of the lever. This acute sensation takes a bit to get used to, and a few corners were undeservingly skidded during our dry summer months before I figured out the bite point-to-traction ratio later on.

Another intended spec is the Fox 36 SL Performance Grip. It’s only got three options for compression: Open, Medium, and Firm, and 17 rebound clicks. Initially, when I had Rusty at the Broken Spoke build up the bike, I’d brought a 36 SL Grip-X fork, thinking I’d want more adjustment and fine-tuning on the Solstice. Much like the Grip-X 34 I’d ridden on the Retrotec, I found that I value Fox’s LSC adjustment for hardtails to ensure proper support.

After the first ride, however, my perspective quickly changed, favoring the simplicity of the Fox 36 SL Performance Grip package. Setting the settings dead center on the rebound and compression in the Open position all the time, I never touched the fork throughout the three-month review period and hundreds of miles of singletrack.

A Parts to the Whole Equation

Yes, powerful brakes and a no-bullshit fork go a long way, as does a familiar-feeling cockpit and drivetrain. It makes it easier to evaluate the bike you’re reviewing, and familiarity makes for a more fulfilling experience. I didn’t have to get used to new tires, or a new drivetrain, or worry about bashing around on some new-to-me wheels. I could focus on what makes the Solstice such a capable and damn fun bike.

Displaying what I believe is the penultimate mountain bike setup – the ultimate being a 120/140 full suspension – my Solstice build achieves a balance of keeping things relatively light while maintaining realistic dependability and durability. All of that works in favor of a frame with just the right amount of wiggle and shimmy.

Riding the Solstice reminded me how much I love hardtails: their simplicity, honesty, and, when done right, capability. I never felt undergunned to the point of checking myself, nor did I wish I’d grabbed a full suspension. A lot of that has to do with how I know the line on every trail in my backyard, so there’s an operator’s efficiency to the equation; but had I ridden unfamiliar terrain, the bike’s familiarity would have helped me just as much, ending my ride unscathed.

Neuhaus got the parts to the whole equation dialed on this frame. The tubing spec, details, and ride feel are dialed. Even the enamel mug blue-inspired paint grew on me! I don’t say this often – and if I do, someone in the comments will undoubtedly correct me – but this is my favorite Taiwan-made steel hardtail I’ve ever ridden.

If it had come in Desert Tan, I might not send it back!

TL;DR

In a mountain bike industry that treats the hardtail as a novelty or beginner’s bike, it’s nice to see brands like Neuhaus Metalworks put their heart and soul into a bike like the Solstice. Equally at home in Marin County or in the rough and rugged Sangre de Cristo Mountains of New Mexico, this bike has the heart to be pushed to the limits, while offering plenty of clearance for big rubber, a burly fork, and powerful brakes. Its chassis flexes in just the right amount, coming in at “Cotta” on our frame flex pasta cook chart.

I’d recommend buying it as a frame with the Fox 36 SL Performance Grip fork, since I think it’s a perfect pairing, and then swapping in your parts. Of course, for Neuhaus, they would prefer to sell a complete to you, but if you’re being budget-conscious, I think the frame and fork package price of $1,899 is a fair consideration. Maybe spring for those TRP brakes too if you like instant, immediate power.

Three years ago, I saw a rolling prototype of this bike and fell in love; now, after this review period, my heart is full of admiration for what the team has achieved. I know this all sounds hella cheesy, but I’m being sincere here. The Solstice remains mild-mannered, collected, and cool when it needs to be, but it can also be wielded like a broadsword in the battle of Osgiliath on descents. It’s a simple but capable hardtail; nothing more, nothing less.

Pros

  • Progressive-ish geo
  • Appealing price
  • Flexy (in a good way) frame
  • 130 mm is just enough travel to get rowdy on
  • 2.6″ tire clearance
  • Lightweight at 6.7 lbs for the frame and 32 lbs complete as shown

Cons

  • No sliding dropouts for single-speeders
  • Some might say it’s expensive for a steel frame hardtail
  • Seat stay bridge could use like 5 mm more clearance
  • Geo might not be progressive enough for some riders

Check out more at Neuhaus Metalworks.
